content: Dried fruit refers to fruit that has undergone a dehydration process, either naturally or through the use of specialized equipment such as a dehydrator. Common examples of dried fruits include raisins, prunes, and dates. Other fruits that can be dried include apples, apricots, bananas, cranberries, figs, kiwis, mangoes, pawpaw, peaches, pears, persimmons, pineapples, strawberries, and even tomatoes. Dried fruit is known for its extended shelf life, making it a practical alternative to fresh fruit, especially for out-of-season varieties. The drying process is an effective method of preserving fruit in the absence of refrigeration. Dried fruit is frequently incorporated into baking mixes and breakfast cereals due to its convenience and flavor. Nutritionally, dried fruits are rich in vitamins such as A, B1, B2, B3, B6, and pantothenic acid, as well as essential dietary minerals including calcium, iron, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, copper, and manganese. On average, dried fruit contains approximately 250 calories and 1–5 grams of protein per 100 grams. The dehydration process results in significant water loss, often up to seven-eighths of the fruit's original water content, which intensifies the flavor of the dried product. However, this process also leads to the destruction of most of the fruit's Vitamin C content, leaving the dried version with only a fraction of the Vitamin C levels found in fresh fruit. Commercially prepared dried fruits may contain added sulfur dioxide, a preservative used to maintain the product's color. However, sulfur dioxide can trigger asthma in sensitive individuals. For those seeking alternatives, sulfur-free dried fruits are available, particularly in health food stores. Organic dried fruits, which are produced without sulfur, tend to have a darker appearance and a flavor profile that more closely resembles that of fresh fruit. In addition to whole dried fruits, fruit purées can also be dehydrated to create fruit leather, a chewy and concentrated fruit product.
